dialogs.title: Диалог — An evening at the механа
dialogs.intro: Ani and Maria have dinner at a *механа*, a traditional Bulgarian tavern. Watch the pronoun form after the preposition **за** — the short form is not allowed there.

lines.speaker: Сервитьор:
lines.id: Good evening! Here you are, the menu.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Thank you. What would you recommend for us?

lines.speaker: Сервитьор:
lines.id: The shopska salad is very good. And the moussaka.
lines.literal: shopska-the — salad — is — very — good. and — moussaka-the.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: OK. One shopska salad and one banitsa, please.
lines.literal: OK. one — shopska — salad — and — one — banitsa, please.

lines.speaker: Мария:
lines.id: A glass of red wine for me.

lines.speaker: Мария:
lines.id: Cheers! Look me in the eye!

notes: ⚠️ **After a preposition, a pronoun MUST take the long form.** *За мен*, not *за ме*. *С теб*, not *с те*. *На него*, not *на му*. The short forms you learned in Unit 6 can only cling directly to a verb; as soon as a preposition comes before them, they switch to the long form.
**За мен … is the shortest and most common way to order.** No verb needed at all: *За мен таратор.* It is also how orders get divided up at a big table.
**Наздраве means "to health" and is used for two things**: toasting, and speaking to someone who sneezes — just like *Gesundheit* in German, which English speakers borrow too.

⚠️ **A Bulgarian toast requires eye contact.** When the glasses clink, look into the eyes of the person you are toasting — not at the glass. Skipping it is considered rude, or at least odd, and an old superstition says it brings seven years of bad luck. Just watch a group toasting: every head turns to find everyone else's eyes.

**Read a menu by its sections, not word by word.** *Салати* (salads), *предястия* (starters), *основни ястия* (main courses), *гарнитури* (sides), *десерти* (desserts), *напитки* (drinks). If you recognize just these six words, you can navigate any menu in Bulgaria.

**Сметката, моля is the closing line that always works.** You can also mime writing in the air, a gesture understood all over Bulgaria. ⚠️ A tip (**бакшиш**) is about ten percent and is usually left on the table, not handed over.
**Веднага means "right away, immediately".** You will hear it a lot from waiters, and it is about as flexible as "just a minute" in English.

**The vowel о in вкусно, вино, много is read as a full o in careful speech**, but in fast talk it leans toward *oo*: *MNO-goo*, *VEE-noo*. Don't be surprised if what you hear isn't exactly what is written.

grammars.title: Three ways to order
body: All three are correct and all three are polite. Pick whichever comes out of your mouth fastest.
after: ⚠️ Note that the number "one" follows the gender of the food: *един чай* (masculine), *една салата* (feminine), *едно кафе* (neuter). Getting it wrong won't stop your order, but getting it right sounds far more practiced.

grammars.title: Long pronoun forms — required after prepositions
body: This second set of pronouns appears in only two places: after prepositions, and when you want to stress who you mean.

head: Person
Short (object)
Long
Example with a preposition
rows: за мен, с мен, на мен

after: The long forms are also used for contrast: *Не него, а нея* — not him, but her.

In conversation, long and short forms sometimes appear together for heavy emphasis: *На мен ми е приятно* — literally "to me to-me it is pleasant". It sounds redundant in translation, but it is very common and perfectly correct.

sections.title: Five dishes you will definitely be offered

head: Bulgarian
Say it
What it is
rows: Tomatoes, cucumbers, peppers and onions, with a mountain of grated white cheese on top. It is white, green and red — the colors of the national flag.
Thin layered pastry filled with white cheese and eggs. The national breakfast; sold on every corner from six in the morning.
A cold soup of yogurt, cucumber, garlic, dill and walnuts. Drunk, not spooned, on the hottest days.
Layers of potato and minced meat, topped with a baked egg-and-yogurt crust. Not the Greek version with eggplant.
Long minced-meat sausages grilled over charcoal, almost always ordered with *шопска салата* and beer.

blocks.text: Two drinks you should know: **ракия** (*ra-KEE-ya*), a strong fruit brandy sipped slowly before the meal with salad — not after; and **айрян** (*ai-RYAN*), thin salty yogurt that beats the heat.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Word traps for English speakers
items: The word **пиле** (*PEE-leh*) means **chicken** — nothing to do with a "pile". And **баница** has nothing to do with "bananas". Quite a few Bulgarian words sound accidentally funny to an English ear — the main thing is not to laugh in the middle of ordering.

On the other hand, here is one Bulgarian pair you really should know: **майка** means "mother" and is pronounced *MAI-ka*, while **лайка** means chamomile. One letter apart, a whole different conversation.

blocks.text: ⚠️ **Аз съм вегетарианец** for a man, **вегетарианка** for a woman. And be prepared: "no meat" is sometimes taken not to include meat broth or a small piece of bacon. The safe sentence: *Изобщо без месо, моля.* (No meat at all, please.)
